properties.note: Slope measured over the grid cell size; cells steeper than the limit, NoData and a 1-cell buffer around them are impassable.

properties.name: Base: start and end of the walk, at stop 1
Possible Inverted Channel
properties.why_habitability: The canyon floor west of and about 150 m below this stop holds a sinuous, raised ridge that the HiRISE team interprets as a possible inverted channel deposit. Inverted channels form when stream sediment is cemented in place by minerals deposited from water, and the softer rock around it later erodes away. Samples of the ridge could test whether liquid water once flowed here.

properties.name: East Wall Layers
properties.why_habitability: This stop is on the eastern side of the canyon, about 160 m above its floor. Gale crater's central mound is built of layered (stratified) material, and the canyon cuts through it, exposing the layers in its walls; sampling layer by layer gives an ordered record of how these deposits built up. The HiRISE team notes the canyon may have been carved by running water.

properties.name: Debris Deposits
properties.why_habitability: The canyon holds debris deposits and levees left by past mass movements. Hughes et al. (2020) find the slopes too low for dry flows, which suggests water was needed to set them moving, likely groundwater seeping out of the slopes. Orbital CRISM spectra indicate the debris is made of polyhydrated (water-bearing) sulfates.

properties.name: Sulfate Strata and Alcoves
properties.why_habitability: The canyon cuts through sulfate-bearing strata, with tributary alcoves on its walls and coarse debris along its floor. Hughes et al. (2019) state that how much water was involved in forming these deposits is still unknown, which makes them a direct target for observation on the ground.

properties.name: Northern Canyon Terrace
properties.why_habitability: The walk ends on terrace ground at the northern end of the route. The layered rock of Gale's central mound is exposed in the canyon walls, and the HiRISE team notes the canyon may have been carved by running water.
